text:
Keep the Joined-Up Hand: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Cursive

Every few years a headline announces the death of handwriting. Keyboards are everywhere, the argument goes, so the hours children spend looping their letters together are hours wasted. Finland has moved much of its writing instruction towards typing, and several American states dropped cursive from their standards before some of them quietly reversed course. It is a tidy story, but I think it is wrong. Primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it properly, not as a decorative leftover from the age of the fountain pen. The case rests on four things: what the skill does for a child's thinking, what it does for their writing speed and comfort, what it does for children who struggle, and what we lose if we let it go.

Begin with the objection, because it deserves a fair hearing. The world children will work in is digital. Almost nobody over the age of twenty-five writes by hand for more than a few minutes a day: a shopping list, a signature, a note on a form. Typing is plainly a more useful adult skill than cursive. Curriculum time is finite, and teachers are asked to cover reading, mathematics, science, computing and more. If a skill is rarely used, why spend scarce hours drilling it?

The answer is that the question assumes handwriting is only a means of producing text. It is also a way of learning, and the evidence for that is stronger than the sceptics tend to admit. Studies in cognitive psychology and neuroscience have repeatedly found that writing by hand engages the brain differently from pressing keys. When a child forms a letter, the hand must make a distinct movement for each shape, and those movements are tied to the visual identity of the letter. Brain imaging work, including research with young children, has shown that handwriting activates networks associated with reading and language more strongly than typing does. Children who learn letters by drawing them tend to recognise them more reliably than children who learn them by tapping a key, where every letter costs the same identical motion. The finger that presses A and the finger that presses B differ only in position. The hand that writes them must reproduce their shapes.

Joined-up writing adds something further. In print, each letter is a separate act, with a lift of the pen between every one. In a joined style, the hand learns whole words as flowing movements. That continuity matters because it turns spelling into something the body remembers. Many adults who write fluently will tell you that they sometimes spell a tricky word by tracing it in the air, because the pattern lives in the hand as much as in the head. Joined writing builds that motor memory for common letter strings such as -ing, -tion and -ght, which are exactly the patterns children find hardest to spell. A skill that reinforces spelling is not a luxury in a primary classroom.

The second argument concerns speed and fluency. A child who has not mastered an efficient, joined style often writes slowly and with effort. This is not a trivial problem. Writing is the main way primary and secondary pupils show what they know, and for years to come it remains the medium of nearly every exam. A pupil whose hand cannot keep pace with their ideas will write shorter answers, choose simpler words, and avoid the long, complex sentences that signal real thought. Researchers who study writing development talk about transcription skills consuming working memory. If forming each letter takes conscious effort, there is less mental capacity left for composition. Automatic handwriting frees the mind to attend to what is being said. Joined-up writing, taught well, is faster than printing because the pen stays on the page and the hand does not stop and start. That speed becomes a real advantage by the age of ten or eleven, when the demands on written output rise sharply.

It is true that a fluent typist can outpace most handwriters, but the realistic comparison for primary pupils is not with a skilled adult typist. Most seven-year-olds type with one or two fingers, slowly and with their eyes on the keys. Touch typing takes many hours of dedicated practice to reach even moderate speed, and schools rarely have the time or the equipment to deliver it to every child. Meanwhile pencil and paper work in any classroom, with no charging, no passwords, no software updates and no distractions. A technology that is always available and cannot send a notification has a quiet virtue.

The third argument is about equity, and it is the one I find most persuasive. Joined-up handwriting is often accused of being elitist or old-fashioned, but the reverse is closer to the truth. Children from homes with plenty of books, devices and spare time will pick up many literacy skills almost regardless of what school does. The children who depend most on explicit teaching are those who have no such cushion. For them, a structured handwriting programme is a clear, learnable, finite skill, and mastering it produces visible success. Pupils with dyslexia and related difficulties are a particularly important case. Specialists have long recommended joined, multisensory handwriting for many of these children, because the continuous movement reduces the confusion between letters such as b and d that are mirror images in print but look and feel quite different when joined. A flowing style gives each letter a clear entry and exit, which makes reversals less likely. If we stop teaching it in the name of modernisation, the children who lose out will be the ones who most needed it.

There is also the matter of dignity and self-presentation. Whether we like it or not, handwriting is read as a signal. Teachers and examiners are human, and research on marking has found that neat, legible scripts tend to receive higher marks than untidy ones for identical content. A child who cannot produce legible writing at speed is handicapped in a way that has nothing to do with intelligence. Teaching a clear joined hand is, among other things, a form of fairness: it gives every child the same tool for being read.

The fourth argument is more cultural, though no less real. Cursive is how we read much of the past. Letters, diaries, wills, registers and recipes were written in joined hands, and a generation that cannot read cursive cannot read its own family archive without a translator. Some American educators have noted, with a certain alarm, that students struggle to read the original text of the Declaration of Independence. This may sound like sentiment, but the cost is practical: if joined writing becomes a skill only specialists possess, then the handwritten record of ordinary lives becomes as inaccessible as a medieval manuscript. Teaching children to write cursive teaches them to read it, and reading it keeps a door open between them and the generations before.

None of this means schools should cling to the methods of the past. The strongest version of my argument is not a plea to bring back hours of copying lines in silence. The better research suggests short, frequent, well-structured sessions are far more effective than long drills. Children should be taught correct posture, a comfortable pencil grip and consistent letter formation from the start, and joins should be introduced once letters are secure, usually around the age of six or seven. The style should be simple. The elaborate looped scripts of the Victorian copybook add difficulty without adding legibility, and a plain, slightly slanted joined hand is easier to learn and quicker to write. Schools should also let children develop their own style as they mature, as nearly all adults do. The aim is fluency and legibility, not a museum piece.

Nor is this an argument against keyboards. Children need to learn to type as well, and the sensible position is that both skills deserve time. A child who can write by hand and can type is better equipped than one who can only do either. The mistake is the either-or framing, the assumption that every new technology must kill the old one. Printing did not abolish speech, and the calculator did not abolish mental arithmetic, though some predicted it would. In each case, teachers eventually concluded that the older skill supported understanding of the newer one. Handwriting supports typing in just this way: children who know the shape and sound of a letter from writing it find that the keyboard is simply a faster way to say what they already know.

There is a final point about attention. A child writing by hand is doing one thing. A child at a screen is a click away from a game, a video, a message. Classrooms that have introduced devices widely often report that managing distraction becomes a large part of the teacher's job. Pencil and paper offer a space in which a child can think without the competing pull of everything else a device can do. That quiet, undivided attention is itself a skill, and one that fewer children are practising each year.

So the case stands. Joined-up handwriting supports the link between letters and sounds, builds spelling through movement, frees working memory for composition, helps the children who find literacy hardest, produces legible writing that is rewarded in the real world, and keeps us in touch with the written past. The cost is a modest amount of well-organised practice in the early years. The benefit is a fluent, comfortable and reliable tool that the child will carry for life, even if they use it less than their grandparents did. A skill does not have to be used all day to be worth having. We teach children to swim without expecting them to live in the water.

The sensible course is not to abandon joined-up handwriting but to teach it with confidence, in a simple style, with short regular practice, and alongside keyboard skills rather than instead of them. Primary schools that do so are not clinging to nostalgia. They are making a sound judgement about what helps young children think, spell, write and be read. The pen is not obsolete. It is simply the first of the tools that a literate person needs.
